title: Be Cool
full_review:
At one point in "Be Cool" (MGM), the flat follow-up to the 1995 comedy "Get Shorty," John Travolta, reprising the role of movie-obsessed mobster-turned-Hollywood player Chili Palmer, shakes his head in disgust and groans, "Sequels!"

Though funny in a self-deprecating way, his near-nauseous reaction pretty much says it all.

Despite an eclectic ensemble cast headed by the ever-affable Travolta, "Be Cool" is, contrary to its title, lukewarm.

As with "Get Shorty," the new film, directed by F. Gary Gray, is based on a novel by pulp fiction icon Elmore Leonard. In it, Chili, having grown disenchanted with the movie industry, turns his sights on another, disreputable by even organized-crime standards: the music business.

When record producer pal Tommy Athens (James Woods) gets bumped off by a follicle-challenged hit man from the Russian mob, Chili agrees to manage Linda Moon (played by pop star Christina Milian), a promising young singer in need of a break. Athens had been trying to get her out of a bad deal that has kept her contractually stuck performing in a sleazy, third-rate girl group.

Aiding Chili in his new venture is Athens' widow and record-producing partner (Uma Thurman), who had always carried a torch for the ex-wise guy. (The two even get to cut a rug in a scene lifted straight out of "Pulp Fiction.")

As in the earlier film, Chili has to use his streetwise skills to navigate a minefield of complications involving such colorful personalities as: Sin LaSalle, an Ivy League-educated gangsta-rap mogul (Cedric the Entertainer), to whom Athens owed money; Dabu (Andre Benjamin of the hip-hop group Outkast), Sin's trigger-happy henchman; Nick Carr (Harvey Keitel), a shady record producer who owns Linda's contract; Raji (Vince Vaughn), Carr's bungling faux-ghetto lackey; and Elliot (The Rock), Raji's gay actor wanna-be bodyguard.

Exuding super-smooth charisma and unflappable confidence, Travolta makes "Be Cool" far more watchable than it deserves to be; nonetheless, much of his performance feels like a "Get Shorty" retread and borders on outright parody of what was already a caricatured role.

While some viewers may find it hard to sympathize with even a reformed gangster, Chili, as played by Travolta, is likable with his gentlemanly sense of fairness. Though he favors a more civil approach to conflict management, he is not above using strong-arm tactics if the situation requires.

In both its writing and visuals, "Be Cool" lacks the hip sharpness and satirical edge of "Get Shorty," and opts for a broader comedy approach.

Several of the main characters from "Get Shorty," including Chili's love interest, Karen (who had been played by Rene Russo), have been dropped, and much of the plot just doesn't ring true given what was established in the first film. Did Chili wake up one morning and decide that he wants out of movies, after spending all of "Get Shorty" trying to get in?

Also missing is John Lurie's jazzy score.

One thing that hasn't changed is the expletive-laden dialogue, which some viewers may find off-putting.

Part of the problem perhaps lies with the source material itself. Leonard seemed on much firmer ground when lampooning the Hollywood film industry -- of which he has enjoyed an intimate insider's view since his Western short story, "3:10 to Yuma," was adapted to the big screen in 1957.

Unlike "Get Shorty" director Barry Sonnenfeld, who juggled the intricacies of Leonard's darkly comic plot with dexterity, Gray fails to keep all the balls in the air.

The movie contains recurring violence, an implied sexual encounter, images of smoking, drug content, some vulgar gestures, and much rough and crude language and humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
